meanings.note: Placed directly before a name or title when addressing someone in Arabic (يا نور 'Nour!', يا أستاذ 'sir!') and in exclamations (يا سلام! 'wonderful!').

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Active participle of سمع ('to hear'), standard in Jordanian for 'can you hear?' (سامعني؟).

examples.trans: I hear you clearly on the phone.
Do you hear the sound of a car outside the gate?

meanings.note: Subject pronoun 'I' for any speaker.

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I am Salma from the kitchen.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بمر, بيمر).

examples.trans: Pass right beside the green pharmacy.

examples.text: أنا مريت من جنب السبيل الحجري!
examples.trans: I just passed the stone fountain!

meanings.note: Everyday preposition meaning 'from', 'of', or 'than' after comparatives.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday word for 'next to, beside'.

examples.trans: Put a napkin beside every cup.
There is no light beside the bed.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: صيدليات.

examples.trans: The green pharmacy is beside the overpass.
I walked past the pharmacy this morning.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: خضرا, plural: خضر).

examples.trans: Pass beside the green pharmacy.
Put the green herbs on the eggs.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: I can hear you clearly on the phone now.
He explained the idea with complete clarity.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: واقفة, plural: واقفين).

examples.trans: There is nobody standing in the courtyard.
They stood face to face under the tree.

meanings.note: Marks location ('at, by') and with pronoun suffixes expresses possession: عندي ('I have'), عندك ('you have'), عندنا ('we have').

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door.
I have a reservation under the name Suad.

meanings.note: In Amman and Levantine cities, سبيل المي is a public stone drinking fountain.

examples.trans: Wait for me by the stone drinking fountain.

examples.text: سبيل الحارة مبني من حجر أبيض.
examples.trans: The neighbourhood fountain is built of white stone.

meanings.note: Universal Jordanian/Levantine word for water (feminine!). Before another noun in possession ('water of...'), becomes مية (mayyet): مية الدوش ('shower water'), مية الشتا ('winter water').

examples.trans: Please drink a glass of cold water.
The hot water is working again in the bathroom.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: حجرية, plural: حجريين).

examples.trans: Go down the stone stairs to downtown.
She stood beside the stone fountain.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: صغيرة, plural: صغار).

examples.trans: We found a little wooden train in the bag.
There are two small streets on the left.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for both casual 'yes / yeah' and 'oh! / ah!' upon noticing something.

examples.trans: Oh, the door opened! Thank you.
Yes, eight rooms and eight keys.

في.gloss: there is; there are; is there?

meanings.en: there is; there are; is there?
meanings.note: Spoken Levantine existential word ('there is / there are'); negated as ما في ('there is no / there are no').

examples.trans: There is a small paper tag on the handle.
There is nobody standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شوارع.

examples.trans: Our guesthouse is on a quiet street in central Amman.
There are old stone streets in the quarter.

meanings.note: In everyday Jordanian directions, شمال (shmaal) means 'left' (contrast شَمال shamaal 'north').

examples.trans: Turn left at the street corner.
The key is on the shelf to your left.

meanings.note: In questions أي means 'which?' (أي علبة؟ 'which tin?'); in conditionals/negatives it means 'any' (أي شي 'anything').

examples.trans: Which tub of butter did you bring?

examples.text: رني الجرس إذا احتجتي أي شي.
examples.trans: Ring the bell if you need anything.

meanings.note: Used both as the numeral 'one' and after a noun for emphasis ('a single, one and the same').

examples.trans: Not a single scratch on the cup!
The gate rang with one strong ring.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (باخد, بياخد).

examples.trans: Someone took my suitcase by mistake!
Old buildings take time to warm up.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: تانية, plural: تانيين).

examples.trans: Room four is on the second floor.
There is a second sheet behind the letter.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أكشاك.

examples.trans: The flower stall is on the corner of the street.
I bought a paper from the little kiosk.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ورد.

examples.trans: We walked past the flower stall.
The scent of roses and jasmine filled the courtyard.

meanings.note: Negates nouns, adjectives, participles, and pronouns in spoken Jordanian (مش شنتتي 'not my bag', مش ملاقي 'cannot find').

examples.trans: This is not my suitcase!
Not bad for a second day at work!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أزقة.

examples.trans: The stone alley is narrow and quiet.
We turned past the narrow lane.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: ضيقة, plural: ضيقين).

examples.trans: The attic stairs are a bit narrow.
Do not enter the narrow alley.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian presentative word ('here is! / look!') pointing to someone or something right now; takes suffixes (هيهم hayy-hum 'here they are!').

examples.text: هي تاكسي وقف عند الباب هلا!
examples.trans: Look, a taxi just stopped at the door!
Here they come down the stairs!

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.text: الشارع على بعد خمس دقايق مشي.
examples.trans: The street is five minutes away on foot.
Walking in the morning in Amman is enjoyable.

meanings.note: Exclamation of mild surprise or realization ('oh!').

examples.trans: Oh! My glasses are on my head!
Oh, look at the beauty of this ceiling!

meanings.note: Active participle of شاف ('to see'), standard in Jordanian for 'I see / do you see?'.

examples.text: شايفة رسمة المفتاح الدهبي فوق الباب!
examples.trans: I see the painted golden key above the door!
Do you see the yellow light in the attic window?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: رسمات.

examples.text: في رسمة مفتاح دهبي فوق الباب.
examples.trans: There is a drawing of a golden key above the door.
His pencil sketches are very detailed.

meanings.note: Means both a door key and a mechanic's spanner/wrench (مفتاح حديد iron wrench).

examples.trans: Here is the key to room four.
We have eight brass keys on the board.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: دهبية, plural: دهبيين).

examples.trans: The gold tin is on the top shelf.

examples.text: فوق الباب في رسمة مفتاح دهبي.
examples.trans: Above the door there is a painted golden key.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: بواب.

examples.trans: The wooden door is open now.
Someone knocked on the door.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: زرقا, plural: زرق).

examples.trans: The blue suitcase is in the luggage closet.
I have two blue teacups.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: ممتازة, plural: ممتازين).

examples.trans: The reading light beside the desk is excellent.
The shower water was hot and excellent!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مفتوحة, plural: مفتوحين).

examples.trans: Is the hardware shop open right now?
Here is to neighbours and our open gates!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بفتح, بيفتح).

examples.trans: The corner shop opens at seven.
Oh, the door finally opened!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: قفال.

examples.trans: The shopkeeper unlocked the padlock in the morning.
We fitted a new brass lock on the closet.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word for 'now / right now' (pronounced halla' in Amman).

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door now.
We will check the tag right now.

meanings.note: Very frequent Jordanian verb: خليني ('let me'), خلينا ('let us'), خليك ('stay!'), خلي ('keep/leave').

examples.trans: Let us open the door together.
Hot bread makes people pleasant!

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'with'; takes pronoun suffixes to express 'have on one's person' (معي 'I have with me', معك حق 'you are right').

examples.trans: You are right, Nour!
Goodbye! (lit. go with safety)

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: خطوط.

examples.trans: Your handwriting on the card is clear and neat.
Stay with me on the line a second.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ثواني.

examples.trans: Wait one second, please.
He came back ten seconds later on the dot.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بتأكد, بيتأكد).

examples.trans: I am just checking safety.
Make sure the size is twenty millimetres.

meanings.note: Introduces 'that'-clauses with pronoun suffixes (إنه 'that', إني 'that I', إنك 'that you', إنها 'that she/it') and appears in إن شاء الله ('if God wills').

examples.trans: Thank you for coming today.
Do you think that I am a hotel inspector?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: حلقات.

examples.trans: The brass ring is twenty millimetres wide.
We fitted a new washer on the pipe.

meanings.note: In Jordanian Arabic, نحاس covers both yellow brass and red copper, often placed directly after a noun (مفاتيح نحاس brass keys).

examples.trans: We polished the brass keys in the morning.
The brass pot is old and engraved.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('inside the bag') and standalone ('inside').

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
The water is flowing inside!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: عروض.

examples.trans: He measured the width of the courtyard.
The ring is twenty millimetres wide.

meanings.note: Numeral 'twenty' (followed by a singular noun in Arabic: عشرين دقيقة 'twenty minutes').

examples.trans: We need twenty eggs for breakfast.
The ring's width is twenty millimetres.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مليمترات.

examples.trans: The ring width is twenty millimetres exactly.
He measured the part to the millimetre.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقيس, بيقيس).

examples.trans: I measure quietness and acoustics in courtyards.
The shopkeeper measured it against the old valve.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: قديمة, plural: قدام).

examples.trans: The courtyard has an old jasmine tree.
The old hardware shop is past the bridge.

meanings.note: Active participle of ضل ('to remain'); standard Jordanian for 'there is ... left'.

examples.trans: He has two valves left on the shelf.
How much time is left until noon?

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian numeral 'two' (إنتو التنين 'the two of you'); note homograph التنين ('Monday').

examples.trans: He has two left on the shelf.
Hold the torch, the two of you!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: رفوف.

examples.trans: The gold tin is on the top shelf.
There are two pieces left on the shelf.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بشتري, بيشتري).

examples.trans: Tell me exactly what to buy.
Buy both brass valves together.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: صمامات.

examples.trans: We fitted a new brass valve on the boiler.
Make sure the valve is tightly shut.

meanings.note: Often placed directly after a noun in Jordanian to mean 'spare' (مفتاح احتياط a spare key).

examples.trans: I have a spare key in the drawer.
We bought a spare valve for winter.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بنقذ, بينقذ).

examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast!
You saved my whole trip.

meanings.note: In Jordanian Arabic, شتا means both the winter season and rain.

examples.trans: Winter water is very cold in the morning.
I love the sound of winter rain on the window.

meanings.note: Active participle of إجا ('to come'): means 'on the way / arriving' (جايين 'they are coming') and after a time noun 'next' (الأسبوع الجاي 'next week').

examples.trans: The guests are coming down the stairs now.
We will see you next week!

كمان.gloss: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)

meanings.en: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)
meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'also, too, more' (كمان مرة 'one more time / again').

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بدفع, بيدفع).

examples.trans: Lift the handle first and then push.
I paid for both valves in cash!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: I paid the bill in cash at the shop.
Do you prefer paying cash or card?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: صناديق.

examples.trans: The screwdriver is inside the toolbox.
We moved four boxes out of the hallway.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: عدد.

examples.trans: The screwdriver and wrench are in the toolbox.
He brought the tools to fix the boiler.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: راجعة, plural: راجعين).

examples.trans: I am running right back across the bridge now!
Salma is coming back from the table.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: She came running back across the overpass in ten minutes.
Running in the morning energises the body.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: جسور.

examples.trans: Cross the overpass toward downtown.
The old shop is past the overpass.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بستعجل, بيستعجل).

examples.trans: Hurry, the guests are coming down the stairs!
Do not rush to go upstairs.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسمع, بيسمع).

examples.trans: Did you hear the gate bell downstairs?
Inside the courtyard we hear the tree leaves.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: خطوات.

examples.trans: I heard footsteps on the wooden stairs.
We walked step by step in the rain.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'on, at, to'; before ال- it regularly contracts to عال- ('al- / 'a-).

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Unvocalised درج covers both daraj ('stairs', masculine collective) and durj ('desk drawer').

examples.trans: Go up the stairs to the second floor.
The big notebook is inside the drawer.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: طوابق.

examples.trans: Your room is on the second floor on the right.
The building has three storeys.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.
